title: The Promises and Pitfalls of LLMs as Feedback Providers: A Study of Prompt Engineering and the Quality of AI-Driven Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can generate high-quality instructional feedback and what prompt characteristics are needed to elicit that quality. The authors are motivated by the broader challenge in higher education that expert feedback is time-consuming, while novice feedback is often lower in quality. They therefore develop a theory-driven prompt engineering manual and compare feedback produced by ChatGPT-4 under three prompts of varying quality.

The intervention studied is not a school-based coaching program, but an LLM feedback workflow in which ChatGPT-4 is prompted to comment on a learning goal containing three intentional errors. The researchers first code and compare LLM outputs across low-, medium-, and high-quality prompts, then use the best-performing prompt to elicit feedback from novice pre-service teachers and expert educators for comparison. The population is higher-education actors in teacher education: pre-service teachers, teacher trainers, educational science professors, and a headmaster, all working with a teacher-education feedback task.

The study finds that prompt quality strongly shapes feedback quality: only the best prompt reliably produced strong LLM feedback, while a superficially good prompt could still generate hallucinated errors. Overall, ChatGPT-4 outperformed novice feedback and in some dimensions even exceeded expert feedback, especially in specificity, questions, and explanations. The authors conclude that LLMs can be efficient and high-quality feedback providers in higher education, but only when guided by careful prompting and human oversight; they also emphasize ethical concerns such as privacy, data security, and the need for experts to monitor and revise AI-generated feedback.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based chatbot/LLM system used to generate feedback from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as ChatGPT-4 to generate feedback on a learning goal given prompts of varying quality, and then compared against novice and expert feedback.

findings.finding_summary: Using three prompt variants, ChatGPT-4 produced feedback that differed significantly by prompt quality. The highest-quality prompt (prompt 3) yielded better feedback than prompts 1 and 2 on assessment criteria, explanation, first person, questions, explanation of suggestions, and specificity; prompt quality was also associated with fewer errors than prompt 2. Sample sizes for this part were 20 feedback instances per prompt (n=60 total).
findings.measure: Feedback quality subdimensions coded with a prompt manual and content analysis (assessment criteria, explanation, first person, questions, explanation of suggestions, specificity, errors)
findings.effect_size: MDiff values reported: assessment criteria 1.50 vs prompt 1 and 0.90 vs prompt 2; explanation 0.75 vs prompt 1 and 0.40 vs prompt 2; first person 1.05 vs prompt 1 and 0.95 vs prompt 2; questions 0.70 vs prompt 1 and 1.00 vs prompt 2; explanation of suggestion 0.60 vs prompt 1; specificity 1.25 vs prompt 1; errors prompt 2 vs prompt 1 MDiff = -0.85 and vs prompt 3 MDiff = -0.95
findings.confidence_interval: Multiple 95% CIs reported in text for pairwise prompt comparisons, e.g. assessment criteria 95% CI [1.10, 1.90] vs prompt 1 and [0.50, 1.30] vs prompt 2; other CIs not fully repeated here

findings.finding_summary: Compared with novice and expert feedback, ChatGPT-4 feedback generated using the highest-quality prompt was superior to novice feedback across all subdimensions except valence and first person. Relative to expert feedback, ChatGPT-4 was significantly better in explanation, questions, and specificity. The comparison included 30 novice feedback instances, 11 expert feedback instances, and 30 LLM feedback instances.
findings.measure: Feedback quality subdimensions coded with the same feedback quality scheme
findings.effect_size: MDiff values reported vs experts: explanation 0.46, questions 0.50, specificity 0.96; versus novices, no effect sizes were reported in the summary text
findings.confidence_interval: For expert comparisons: explanation 95% CI [0.17, 0.74], questions 95% CI [0.07, 0.93], specificity 95% CI [0.52, 1.41]
findings.sample_size: n=30 LLM feedback, n=30 novice feedback, n=11 expert feedback

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single empirical comparative study using coded feedback outputs rather than a randomized field trial. The methodology is quantitative and reasonably clear, but it is situated in a higher-education prompt/feedback task rather than a school implementation study.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported differences are substantively meaningful, with several moderate-to-large mean differences in feedback quality subdimensions and clear advantages for higher-quality prompts. However, the paper does not report a single standardized effect size like d, so impact is best treated as modest-to-moderate rather than definitive.
